a: on the twelfth day of the month
p: The first Egypt oracle comes while Jerusalem is under siege, and about a year before the city falls.
b: Ezekiel counts years from Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC, so the tenth year is 588/587 BC and the tenth month falls about January 587. The tenth day of the tenth month of the year before was the day the siege began (24:1-2; 2 Kings 25:1), so this word comes about a year into it. Egypt had sent an army to help Zedekiah, and the Babylonians had pulled back for a time (Jeremiah 37:5-11). This oracle says Egypt will not save anyone. Six of the book's thirteen dates sit in chapters 29 to 32, and they are not in order: 29:17 is the latest (571 BC). Some scholars date Jerusalem's fall to 587 rather than 586 BC, which moves every date here by a year; this site follows 586.
r: Ezekiel 24:1-2; Ezekiel 30:20; Ezekiel 31:1; Ezekiel 32:1; Ezekiel 32:17; 2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 37:5-11; Jeremiah 52:4

p: Ezekiel never names him, but the king in 588 to 570 BC was Hophra, whom the Greeks called Apries.
b: Ezekiel says only "Pharaoh king of Egypt." The throne was held in these years by Wahibre Hophra (Greek Apries), who reigned from about 589 to 570 BC. Jeremiah names him (Jeremiah 44:30) and says he will be handed over to his enemies, as Zedekiah was. His army's march toward Jerusalem in 588/587 is what lies behind Jeremiah 37:5-11 and Ezekiel 17:15-17. He lost his throne to his general Amasis in 570 BC; the sources for his end are uneven (Herodotus, Histories 2.161-169; Spalinger's survey of Egypt and Babylon in these years). Ezekiel's seven Egypt oracles are the book's longest run against any single nation; compare Jeremiah 46 and Isaiah 19.

p: Pharaoh is a crocodile or chaos monster in his Nile. Isaiah and Psalm 74 call the same creature a dragon.
b: The Hebrew is ha-tannim, an odd plural form of tannin, a big water creature. Genesis 1:21 has "great sea monsters," and Isaiah and Psalm 74 call the chaos monster God defeats a "dragon" (Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9; Psalm 74:13). Here the picture is first of all the Nile crocodile lying in its channels. Herodotus (Histories 2.70) describes hunters catching crocodiles with a baited hook, which fits the hook in 29:4. But the old chaos-monster language is behind it too: Egypt is named Rahab in other prophets (Isaiah 30:7; Psalm 87:4). The Greek here says "the great dragon." The Plain English Translation says "sea monster" so a reader sees the same word as in Genesis 1:21 and Jeremiah 51:34.
r: Genesis 1:21; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9; Psalm 74:13; Job 41:1; Jeremiah 51:34; Ezekiel 32:2; Revelation 12:3

p: The Hebrew says Pharaoh claims to have made himself. The Greek and many versions smooth it to "I made it."
b: The verb is 'asitani, "I made me." Here Pharaoh says the Nile is his and that he made himself. In 29:9 the Hebrew says only "I made" with no object, and the Plain English Translation adds "it." There the Hebrew also has the third person ("he said"), which the Plain English Translation keeps; the Greek has "you said." The Greek reads "I made them" (the rivers) in both places. Most translations also read "I made it for myself." The Hebrew is bolder: a king who claims to have made himself is claiming what only God can. Commentators compare the story Herodotus tells of Apries (Histories 2.169), a king so sure of his rule that no god, it was said, could remove him. Whether the line quotes a real boast or is Ezekiel's own mockery cannot be known.

p: God hooks Pharaoh as he hooked Assyria, and nets him in chapter 32.
b: The hook in the jaws is a picture of being led where you did not choose. God says the same to Assyria's king: a hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth (2 Kings 19:28; Isaiah 37:29). Ezekiel uses it again for Gog (38:4). The fish sticking to the monster's scales are Pharaoh's subjects and allies, hauled out with him. The net in 32:3 belongs to the same hunter's scene. Ezekiel has already pictured God spreading a net over Zedekiah (12:13; 17:20) and the nations netting a young lion (19:8), so the hunted ruler is a repeated figure in the book.
r: 2 Kings 19:28; Isaiah 37:29; Job 41:1; Ezekiel 12:13; Ezekiel 17:20; Ezekiel 19:8; Ezekiel 32:3; Ezekiel 38:4

a: no one will pick you up or gather you
p: To lie unburied for animals and birds was the curse of the covenant and the shame of kings.
b: Being left on open ground, unburied, was the covenant curse (Deuteronomy 28:26) and is a refrain in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:33; 8:2; 16:4; 25:33). For an Egyptian king it was a special horror, because Egypt spent more care on the burial and afterlife of its kings than any other land. The bodies of the fish of the Nile lie scattered with him. The thought returns in 32:4-6 and in the descent to Sheol in 32:17-32, where the fallen are laid with honor or with shame according to how they were buried.

a: Then all who live in Egypt will know that I am the LORD
p: "They will know that I am the LORD" was said of Egypt at the Exodus. Here it comes round again.
b: This is Ezekiel's refrain (first explained earlier in the book). In chapters 29 to 32 the Hebrew has "know that I am the LORD" in nine verses (29:6, 9, 16, 21; 30:8, 19, 25, 26; 32:15) and "I, the LORD, have spoken" in a tenth (30:12). Egypt is where the formula began. At the Exodus, Egypt was told "the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 7:5; 14:4). Now the same nation hears it again, this time at the end of its power. In 29:16 the Hebrew has "that I am the Lord GOD" (Adonai YHWH) instead, and in 29:21 it is Israel that will know.
orig: וְיָדְעוּ כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה (veyad'u ki ani YHWH)

p: Egypt as a reed that snaps under the hand that leans on it was a saying before Ezekiel.
b: The Assyrian field commander used the same picture to Hezekiah: Egypt is a crushed reed that goes into the hand of the man who leans on it and pierces it (Isaiah 36:6). Ezekiel adds the cause: the house of Israel leaned on Egypt against Babylon (17:15-17; Isaiah 30:1-5; 31:1-3), and each time Egypt failed. The reed grows in the Nile marshes, so the image fits the land. The sin charged is not only failed help but misplaced trust: Israel was to trust the LORD alone.

p: The Hebrew for the last verb can mean "made stand" or "made shake," and the Greek has "broke."
b: The Hebrew verb is he'emadta, "you made stand." Many readers take it as a form of a verb meaning "make shake" or "make stagger," as in Psalm 69:23 where hips are made to shake, and the Plain English Translation follows that sense. The Greek has "you broke all their loins." Either way, the sense is that the reed hurts the man who leans on it. A second small difference: the Hebrew is written "by your hand" but read "by the hand" (a written form and a reading tradition that disagree, called Ketiv and Qere); the sense is the same.

t: Migdol and Syene: north to south
p: The KJV reads a tower of Syene. The Hebrew has two place names that mark the whole length of Egypt.
b: Migdol was a border fortress in the northeast Delta (Jeremiah 44:1; 46:14) and Syene is Aswan on the southern border near Cush. The KJV took migdol as the common noun "tower" and read "the tower of Syene." The Greek keeps two names, "Migdol and Syene." The same words occur in 30:6, where the Plain English Translation gives them the same way. Near Syene, on the island of Elephantine, a Jewish military colony lived in the 400s BC and left Aramaic letters and contracts (Porten); how long before that Judeans had lived there is not known. The whole phrase says the ruin will run from one end of the land to the other.

t: Forty years of emptiness: what did it mean?
p: Egypt was not empty for forty years. The number has been read several ways.
b: No record shows Egypt without people for forty years. The views: (1) The number is a round figure, as in the forty years in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33-34), meaning a full generation of punishment; many commentators take it this way. (2) It is literal but fulfilled in a way history does not record; Josephus says that Nebuchadnezzar attacked Egypt in his twenty-third year (Antiquities 10.9.7), but a desolation of the whole land is not found in any source. (3) Rashi ties it to the forty years left of the forty-two years of famine decreed in Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41). (4) Critical readers see a prophecy that did not come true as stated, left in the book as it was. See also 29:17-21.

p: The same phrase is used for Israel's return, for Sodom (16:53) and here for Egypt.
b: The Hebrew is shuv shevut, which can be read "turn back the captivity" or, from a related word, "turn the fortunes." It is a stock phrase for restoration after disaster. It is said of Israel (Ezekiel 39:25; Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3), of Sodom (Ezekiel 16:53) and of Egypt here and in Jeremiah 46:26. Jeremiah promises that "people will settle there again, as in the days of long ago" (Jeremiah 46:26). Ezekiel limits the promise: Egypt returns to Pathros, the south (Isaiah 11:11; Jeremiah 44:1; Ezekiel 30:14), as a "lowly kingdom." Isaiah goes furthest: the LORD calls Egypt "my people" (Isaiah 19:25).

p: Egypt never again ruled an empire in the Near East, though it kept its own identity.
b: After Hophra, native kings held Egypt until Persia conquered it in 525 BC. Native pharaohs ruled again from 404 to 343 BC, and then Persians, Alexander (332 BC) and the Ptolemies took over. Egypt never again ruled Canaan and Syria as it had in the days of Thutmose and Ramesses. Readers who take 29:15 as fulfilled point to this long run of foreign rule. Others note that Egypt was prosperous under the Ptolemies and Rome, and say "lowly" is relative. The verse speaks of a kingdom that will not lift itself above the nations again, which is a claim about empire, not wealth.

t: April 571 BC: the latest date in the book
p: This oracle comes after the rest of chapters 29 to 32 and corrects what Ezekiel said about Tyre.
b: The twenty-seventh year is 571 BC and the first day of the first month is about the end of April. It is the latest date in the book, fifteen years after the fall of Jerusalem and two years after the vision of the new Temple (40:1). The oracle is placed here, out of order, because it belongs with Egypt. It answers the siege of Tyre, which Ezekiel foretold in 26:7-14 and which ended after about thirteen years (Josephus, Against Apion 1.21, quoting Menander of Ephesus; Katzenstein).
r: Ezekiel 26:7-14; Ezekiel 40:1; Josephus, Against Apion 1.21; Ezekiel 30:20

p: Besieging soldiers wore off their hair under helmets and rubbed their shoulders raw carrying earth and timber.
b: The Hebrew says each head was "made bald" and each shoulder "made bare" (or "peeled"). Rashi explains that this is what happens to men who besiege a city for many days, carrying loads of wood and stones. The helmet rubs the hair off and the baskets of earth for the siege ramp rub the skin off the shoulder. The prophet is not speaking of mourning, as the same words could in another place, but of work.

a: no wages from Tyre for him or for his army
t: Ezekiel admits a prediction fell short
p: The oracle itself says the siege of Tyre did not pay. Readers explain that in several ways.
b: Chapter 26 foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would break Tyre's walls and plunder it. Here, after the siege, the LORD says the army got no wages. The views: (1) The plain reading, held by many commentators, is that Ezekiel himself says the Tyre prophecy came out differently than expected, and gives Egypt in its place. This is not a modern discovery; the book says it. (2) Rashi says Tyre fell in Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year, but the sea washed away the booty after it was taken. (3) It is often suggested that the Tyrians moved their wealth to the island city before the end. (4) Critics see the oracle as the writer's own revision, inserted to correct earlier words. Josephus, quoting Menander, reports that Tyre later had rulers sent from Babylon (Against Apion 1.21). None of the ancient sources describes a plundering.
r: Ezekiel 26:7-14; Ezekiel 27:1-36; Josephus, Against Apion 1.21; Josephus, Antiquities 10.11.1

a: I am about to give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
p: A Babylonian tablet records a clash with Egypt in 568/567 BC. Nothing shows a conquest.
b: A Babylonian tablet (British Museum 33041) says that in Nebuchadnezzar's thirty-seventh year, 568/567 BC, he marched against Egypt and fought its king, whom it names Amasis; the text is broken and says nothing of what followed (translated in Pritchard, Ancient Near Eastern Texts). Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar invaded Egypt in his twenty-third year, 582 BC, and put to death its king (Antiquities 10.9.7), a report no Egyptian or Babylonian source backs. Jeremiah foretold the same campaign: "about the time when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon would come and strike the land of Egypt" (Jeremiah 46:13). Whether Nebuchadnezzar took Egypt, raided it or fought only at the border is debated.

t: God's use of a foreign king
p: Nebuchadnezzar is paid with Egypt for serving the LORD's purpose without knowing it.
b: Ezekiel does not call Nebuchadnezzar the LORD's servant, as Jeremiah does (Jeremiah 25:9; 27:6; 43:10). But he says the LORD pays him wages, as a master pays a worker, for work done "for me." The reading that history is moved by God even through rulers who do not know him runs through the prophets, as with Assyria (Isaiah 10:5-15) and Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1-7). Jewish and Christian readers agree on the point and differ on how far it excuses the king. The Hebrew says "they" acted for me: the king and the army.

a: make a horn grow for the house of Israel
p: A horn is strength. The same verb appears for David's line in Psalm 132, so Jewish and Christian readers hear a king.
b: A horn is an animal's weapon and so a figure for strength and, in time, for a ruler (1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 132:17; Luke 1:69). The verb "make grow" is the one used in Psalm 132:17, where the LORD makes a horn spring up for David, so many readers take this as a promise of a Davidic ruler. Rashi says he has not found an explanation of this verse. He ties "that day" to the end of the forty years of 29:13, which he places in the time of Belshazzar, and takes the horn to be the rise of Persia. (Isaiah 45:13 speaks of Cyrus freeing the exiles.) The Greek has "a horn will rise for the whole house of Israel."
r: 1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 132:17; Luke 1:69; Ezekiel 34:23-24; Ezekiel 37:24-25; Isaiah 45:13

p: The prophet who was silenced is promised speech.
b: Ezekiel was struck mute at the start of his work (3:26-27) and the silence was to last until a survivor came from Jerusalem (24:27; 33:22). The promise of an "open mouth among them" comes in the last dated oracle in the book, 571 BC, and is addressed to him alone. It means he will be able to speak when the word comes true, with authority before the people. Commentators differ on whether the muteness of 3:26-27 was total or only a limit on his speaking except to deliver oracles; see the notes there.

t: The cry before the Day of the LORD
p: The same cry opens Joel's description of the Day of the LORD.
b: The cry is ahah layyom, "Alas for the day." In Joel it comes at the start of the book's picture of the Day (Joel 1:15). Ezekiel's phrasing is close: "the day is near, yes, the day of the LORD is near." Obadiah 15 and Isaiah 13:6 speak the same way about other nations. Ezekiel had already used "the day" for Jerusalem (7:5-12), and now the day is for Egypt and its allies. Which text borrowed from which is debated; the phrase belongs to the prophets' common stock.

t: The allies of Egypt: Cush, Put, Lud, Kub
p: The names are the African and Anatolian peoples who served as Egypt's soldiers.
b: Cush is the land south of Egypt, Put is a people usually taken as Libya, and Lud is debated (Lydia in western Turkey, or an African people), with the Ludites who bent the bow (Jeremiah 46:9). All three were sources of mercenaries for Egypt. "The mixed peoples" (ha-'erev) are foreigners of mixed origin living in the land (Jeremiah 25:20). Kub appears nowhere else in the Bible and its place is unknown; the Plain English Translation keeps the name. The STEPBible word list glosses it "Libya" (and the Greek list below has Libyans), so Libya is one candidate, but the Hebrew is not the usual word for Libya. The Greek reads "Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans," a different list, so the Hebrew names cannot be restored from it with confidence. Compare the nations of 27:10 and 38:5.
r: Genesis 10:6; Genesis 10:13; Jeremiah 46:9; Jeremiah 25:20; Ezekiel 27:10; Ezekiel 38:5

t: Who are the "sons of the land of the covenant"?
p: A puzzling phrase. Rashi takes it as lands in a treaty with Egypt.
b: The Hebrew is benei erets ha-berit, "sons of the land of the covenant." Rashi says they are the lands that made a treaty to help Egypt. Some have suggested Judeans, since Judah had a treaty with Egypt and many had fled there (Jeremiah 43 to 44). A third group holds that the text is damaged. The Greek reads "the sons of my covenant," which would mean Israel, and it is shown as a variant. The reading as allies fits the list best: all of these fall together with Egypt.

t: Messengers by water to carefree Cush
p: Isaiah has Cush send envoys down the Nile in boats. Here God's messengers go up it.
b: The word tsiyyim (ships) is rare (Numbers 24:24; Isaiah 33:21). The picture of messengers going by water to Cush matches Isaiah 18:1-2, where Cush's own envoys travel by sea in boats of reed. In Ezekiel the messengers go out from the LORD's presence, so they are his agents, and what they carry is alarm. "Carefree" (betach) is the word for people who feel safe; Cush, far up the Nile and sure that Egypt's power was a wall, learns it is not.

p: Ezekiel's word gillulim is a mocking name. A different word, elilim, is added beside it.
b: Gillulim, "filthy idols," is Ezekiel's favorite word for idols and appears dozens of times. It looks like a word for dung pellets and sounds like the verb for rolling, so it is probably a deliberate sneer, and the Greek just says eidola, "idols." It is a different word from elilim, "worthless idols," which is Isaiah's word for Egypt's gods too (Isaiah 19:1), and from shiqqutsim, "detestable things." The Plain English Translation keeps them apart. Memphis was the home of Ptah, the craftsman god, and of the Apis bull. The Greek has no idols in this verse; it speaks of nobles and rulers of Memphis.

a: a leader from the land of Egypt
p: The Hebrew is nasi, the title Ezekiel uses for rulers. The KJV says prince.
b: The Plain English Translation renders nasi as "leader" everywhere, as in 19:1 and 34:24. The KJV and many versions say "prince." The Greek has "rulers of Memphis." The claim is that Egypt will no longer have a native ruler of its own. Native kings did rule Egypt again, from 404 to 343 BC, and under Amasis in the years after Ezekiel (to 526 BC), so the line is not a literal claim about every year, and readers differ on how to take it: as a poetic extreme, or as a claim about the end of the old dynastic order.

t: The cities of Egypt in Ezekiel's list
p: Ezekiel names eight Egyptian places, from the delta in the north to Thebes in the south.
b: Zoan is Tanis in the eastern Delta (Isaiah 19:11, 13; 30:4; Psalm 78:12). Thebes (Hebrew No) was the southern capital, sacked by Assyria in 663 BC (Nahum 3:8-10; Kitchen, Third Intermediate Period); Jeremiah calls its god "Amon of Thebes" (Jeremiah 46:25). Sin is Pelusium, the fortress at the Delta's eastern gate. On is Heliopolis, home of the sun god. Pi-beseth is Bubastis. Tahpanhes is the Greek Daphnae, where Jeremiah's refugees settled and where Petrie dug in 1886 at Tell Defenneh (Jeremiah 43:7-9). Pathros is Upper Egypt, the south. The Greek names several of these in Greek forms: Tanis, Diospolis for Thebes (30:14, 16), Heliopolis, Bubastis. It does not agree on Sin: it reads Sais at 30:15 and Syene at 30:16, not Pelusium.
r: Jeremiah 43:7-9; Jeremiah 44:1; Jeremiah 46:14; Jeremiah 46:25; Nahum 3:8-10; Isaiah 19:11-13

p: The Hebrew is hard. Memphis will have trouble that does not wait for darkness.
b: The words are tsarei yomam. Tsar can mean "distress" or "enemy," and yomam is "by day." The Plain English Translation takes it as distress in full daylight: attackers do not need the night. Other readers take it as "daily enemies" or "enemies in daytime," and the Greek has a different line altogether. The sense is clear enough: no safety, not even in the sun.

p: The Hebrew text writes the city's name as Aven, which means wickedness.
b: The Hebrew has Aven, which is On (Heliopolis, the City of the Sun, Genesis 41:45) spelled differently from Genesis 41:45 (the consonants differ, with an added waw, not only the vowels) so that it means "wickedness, idolatry." Hosea uses the same trick for Bethel, calling it Beth-aven (Hosea 10:5). The Plain English Translation gives the usual name. In the second half of the verse the Hebrew says "they" (feminine), which means the cities themselves go into captivity; the Greek reads "the women," which is its own reading.

t: "The day will go dark" or "hold back"
p: The Leningrad text reads "hold back." The Plain English Translation follows the Greek and another pointing of the consonants: "go dark."
b: The consonants are the same either way. The Leningrad Codex points them chasakh (with a sin), "to withhold, hold back," so the day would hold itself back. Pointed chashakh (with a shin) they mean "grow dark," and the Greek has "the day will grow dark." The Plain English Translation follows the Greek and the shin pointing, because a day of cloud (30:3, 18) and darkness at a ruler's fall (32:7-8) is the standing picture. The Masoretic sense is possible, so the variant table shows both.

p: God once broke the bars of Israel's yoke in Egypt. Now Egypt's own are broken.
b: In Leviticus 26:13 the LORD says he broke the bars of Israel's yoke and let them walk upright. Ezekiel uses the same words for the bars Egypt placed on others, and says the LORD will break them in Tahpanhes, where Judean refugees had gone to seek safety in Egypt. The reversal is deliberate: Israel's oppressor will lose its power, and the refuge turns out to be a place of judgment.

t: Spring 587 BC: after Egypt's failed march
p: The arm Ezekiel says was broken is Pharaoh's army, turned back from relieving Jerusalem.
b: The eleventh year is 587/586 BC, and the seventh day of the first month falls in the spring of 587, about a year and a quarter before the city fell in July 586. Egypt's army had marched up to relieve the siege and the Babylonians withdrew for a short time, then returned and drove the Egyptians off (Jeremiah 37:5-11). The words "I have broken" speak of that defeat as already done; what is still to come is the second blow, the breaking of both arms.

t: The arm that cannot hold a sword
p: An Egyptian king was shown with his arm raised to strike. God breaks it.
b: The raised arm of the king, smiting enemies, was the standard picture of Egyptian kingship on temple walls. In Israel the strong arm was the LORD's (Exodus 6:6; Psalm 98:1; Isaiah 51:9). Here God breaks the king's. The picture of a broken arm that was never splinted or bandaged is that of a limb left to heal crooked, so the king can never fight with it again. Moab's "arm" is broken in the same way in Jeremiah 48:25. The two arms of 30:22 are the strong one and the one already broken.

p: One Hebrew word means a crowd, its noise, and its wealth. It is a refrain in these chapters.
b: Hamon is a crowd of people, a throng, the noise a crowd makes, and the wealth that comes with a crowd. In chapters 29 to 32 the Plain English Translation says "multitude" nearly everywhere, because the word is a refrain: Pharaoh and his multitude go down together (31:18; 32:31-32). Twice the sense is clearly property, and there the Plain English Translation says "wealth" (29:19; 30:4). Greek has plethos, "mass." The word is also the root of Hamon-gog in 39:11, "the horde of Gog."

p: Cedars of Lebanon stand for rulers all through the Bible. Daniel 4 has the same tree and the same birds.
b: A tall cedar is a picture of a proud king in Jotham's fable (Judges 9:15), in Isaiah (Isaiah 2:13; 10:33-34; 14:8) and in Ezekiel's own parable of the cedar shoot (17:3, 22-24). Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 4:10-12, 20-22 describes a great tree with birds in its branches, animals in its shade and a command to cut it down. Ezekiel 31 has the same set of images: birds in its boughs, beasts under its branches, nations in its shade (31:6). Assyrian kings boasted of cutting Lebanon's cedars; the cedar is taller than the king who cuts it only until the cutting.
r: Judges 9:15; Isaiah 2:13; Isaiah 10:33-34; Isaiah 14:8; Ezekiel 17:22-24; Daniel 4:10-12

t: A tree fed by the deep
p: The great tree drinks from the primeval deep. The picture belongs to the ancient Near East but has no single source.
b: The deep (tehom) is the water under the earth from which springs and rivers rise (Genesis 1:2; 7:11). A tree watered from it is a tree at the center of the world, like the tree by the stream in Psalm 1 or the trees along the temple river in 47:12. Ancient Near Eastern art shows sacred trees beside water, and the garden of the gods, with its trees, rivers and a great tree that holds up the sky, is a picture found in several cultures. Commentators agree that Ezekiel draws on a shared picture and disagree on how close any one parallel is. No Egyptian or Mesopotamian text matches the chapter.

a: cedars in the garden of God
p: The trees of Eden are the cedar's rivals. The garden is the same as in Genesis, and chapter 28 uses it for Tyre.
b: "The garden of God" and "Eden" (31:9, 16, 18) are the garden of Genesis 2 to 3, planted by the LORD with every tree good for food. Ezekiel has used it for Tyre's king in 28:13 and uses it again for the restored land (36:35). Isaiah 51:3 and Joel 2:3 use it too. Here the trees are rivals who envy the cedar, and in 31:16 and 18 they go down with it to the earth below. The Greek calls it paradeisos, from which comes "paradise." The Plain English Translation follows Genesis in naming it Eden. Readers differ on whether Ezekiel pictures a place that really existed, a myth, or a figure for royal glory.
r: Genesis 2:8-9; Genesis 13:10; Ezekiel 28:13; Ezekiel 36:35; Isaiah 51:3; Joel 2:3

t: The trees of Eden: cypress, cedar, plane
p: Three kinds of tree, none certain. The Plain English Translation reads berosh "cypress" everywhere.
b: The Hebrew names the cedar (erez), the berosh and the armon. Berosh is a tall evergreen, probably cypress, juniper or fir. The Plain English Translation says "cypress" for it here and at Ezekiel 27:5, as at Isaiah 41:19, 55:13 and 60:13; Isaiah 14:8, which this chapter answers (see 31:15), has the same word, and a request is filed to read it "cypresses" there too, so the tree is not certain but the English is the same every time. The armon is the plane tree, as in Genesis 30:37. In the Greek the three are kuparissoi (cypresses, for the cedars), pitues (pines) and elatai (firs), so the Greek names the trees in a different way.

p: The speech changes from "you" to "it" in the middle of the verse. Pharaoh and the tree blur.
b: In Hebrew this verse begins "because you were tall," then says "it set its top" and "its heart grew proud." The Greek has a shift too, but in a different place: "you became great ... and you gave your top ... and I saw when he was lifted up," second person and then third. The shift shows the two figures merging: the tree is Pharaoh, and Pharaoh is the tree. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew shift because it is the hinge between the fable (31:3-9) and its application. In 31:3, 10 and 14 the word for "dense boughs" may also be read "clouds" (see the variant at 31:3).

p: In the story of the tree, the one who cuts it down is the Babylonian king.
b: Assyria's empire fell between 612 BC (Nineveh) and 609 BC (Harran) to the Babylonians and the Medes, led by Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar's father (Nahum 3:1-19; Zephaniah 2:13-15). So in the fable, the ruler who cuts the cedar down is a Babylonian king. In the application to Egypt, he is Nebuchadnezzar (30:10; 32:11). The Hebrew word is el goyim, "a mighty one of nations"; the Greek says "a ruler of nations." The Plain English Translation says "mighty ruler" to avoid using the word "leader," which it keeps for nasi.

p: The word elehem is unclear. The Plain English Translation reads it as "their mighty ones."
b: The Hebrew says "and they will not stand elehem in their height, all drinkers of water." Elehem could be "to them" (the Greek has "against them") or "their mighty ones" (from ayil, a ram or leader), the sense in the Plain English Translation. The verse says that no tree, however well watered and tall, is to stand as a leader among trees on account of its height, because they all end in the Pit. The meaning of the whole verse is clear even if the word is not.

p: A pit or cistern is a figure for the grave and for the world of the dead.
b: The Hebrew bor is a cistern or a pit dug in the ground. In the Psalms "those who go down to the Pit" are the dead (Psalm 28:1; 30:3; 88:4), and Isaiah uses it for the depths of Sheol (Isaiah 14:15, 19). Ezekiel uses it for the dead in 26:20; 28:8 and in chapters 31 and 32 many times. The Plain English Translation writes it with a capital, as in Isaiah 14:15, so that a reader following the word across the Bible sees the same place. The words "the earth below" (literally "the lowest earth") speak of the same region.
r: Psalm 28:1; Psalm 30:3; Psalm 88:4-6; Isaiah 14:15; Isaiah 14:19; Ezekiel 26:20; Ezekiel 28:8

t: The world mourns a fallen king
p: Isaiah has the trees rejoice when a tyrant falls. In Ezekiel they mourn.
b: When Babylon's king falls, Isaiah has the cypresses and the cedars of Lebanon rejoice: "Since the day you lay down, no woodcutter has climbed up to us" (Isaiah 14:8). Ezekiel turns it around: the deep is covered, rivers held back, Lebanon darkened and the trees withered, all in grief for the fallen tree. Then in 31:16 the nations shake at the sound of its fall, and the trees of Eden are comforted in the earth below. The two reactions go together: the great fall in sorrow for those who sheltered under them and in grim comfort for those who feared them.

p: Egypt circumcised. So the word here cannot only mean a foreign people.
b: To Israel, circumcision was the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17). "Uncircumcised" was an insult for outsiders such as the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:26). Yet the Egyptians practiced circumcision, as Herodotus notes (Histories 2.36-37; 2.104), and Jeremiah lists Egypt among nations circumcised in the flesh and uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25-26). So when Ezekiel puts Pharaoh "among the uncircumcised," many commentators take the word as the dead who are shamed and killed by the sword, with no honor in burial, and not as an ethnic label. Others keep it as a plain label for outsiders to Israel, as in 28:10 and 44:7-9. The notes on this word run on through 32:19-32. The word recurs ten times in 32:17-32. Ezekiel used it earlier for Tyre (28:10).

p: A lament (qinah) is a funeral song. Ezekiel sings one for a king who is not yet dead.
b: The qinah is the song of grief for the dead, such as David's for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17-27). Ezekiel has sung laments for the kings of Judah (19:1-14), for Tyre (27:2-36) and the king of Tyre (28:12-19). This one is for Pharaoh, and is a mock funeral: it describes the dead king as already in Sheol while he is still on the throne. The chapter's own label comes in 32:16, which says the daughters of the nations will chant it. The meter of a qinah has a limping rhythm, which English cannot show.

a: You were like a young lion among the nations
t: Lion on land, monster in the water
p: Pharaoh is two animals, and the Hebrew word for "like" may carry a second meaning.
b: The verb nidmeta can mean "you were likened" (the word used in 31:2 and 31:18) or, from a different root, "you were silenced, destroyed." Some readers hear both. The Plain English Translation keeps "like." The two pictures are of the king on land, a young lion among the nations, and in the river, the tannin, as in 29:3. The Greek says "dragon." Egyptian kings were shown as lions and sphinxes, and also as masters of the Nile; Ezekiel breaks both pictures. The young lion was used for Judah's kings in 19:2-9.

p: The word rumeka is found only here. It may mean heap, height, or worms.
b: The Hebrew rumeka appears once and is built on a root for "high." It could be "your height" (your heap of corpses), or it may stand for a similar word for worms or maggots. The Greek has "your blood" in this verse and "your discharge" in the next. The Plain English Translation takes it as what is left of the huge body, "your remains," a safe middle. The next verse's "flowing blood" (tsapatkha, also found only here) is equally rare.

p: Egypt's ninth plague was darkness. The day of the LORD is told in the same picture.
b: The darkening of sun, moon and stars at a ruler's fall belongs to the language of the Day of the LORD (Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10; 3:15; Amos 8:9). Here it falls on Egypt, which makes a pointed echo of the ninth plague, a darkness over Egypt that could be felt (Exodus 10:21-23). Exodus put a deep dark over Egypt and light in Goshen. Ezekiel does not say that anyone will have light. For the Egyptians, the sun was a god (Re), so darkness over the land also said that Re had failed.
r: Exodus 10:21-23; Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10; Joel 3:15; Amos 8:9; Ezekiel 30:18; Joel 2:31; Matthew 24:29; Revelation 6:12-13

p: The Nile that Pharaoh churned runs smooth like oil. Isaiah 19 says it will dry up.
b: The picture is of silence: no foot or hoof muddies the water, and it settles and runs smoothly. It sits strangely beside the rest of the chapter. It is a peace made of absence, not blessing: nobody is left to stir the river. Isaiah foretold that the Nile would dry up and its fishermen mourn (Isaiah 19:5-10), and Ezekiel says it himself in 30:12. The Nile turned to blood in the first plague (Exodus 7:19-21). The Greek has the rivers "going like oil."

t: The prophet sends the multitude down
p: The prophet is told to bring Egypt down to the Pit by speaking.
b: The command is hordehu, "bring it down." The prophet does not just announce the descent; his word is the means. In Jeremiah, too, the LORD sets the prophet "over nations" "to pull down" (Jeremiah 1:10). Readers differ on whether this means the prophet's word has power by itself or that it is the LORD's act through the prophet. The "daughters of mighty nations" are the nations' peoples or cities.

p: The word that marks the dead in 32:19-32 first appears in the chant here.
b: From here to the end of the chapter the word 'arelim comes ten times, as the common label of the nations in the Pit. See the note at 31:18 for the two ways it is read: as the dishonored dead (killed by the sword, laid without honor), or as a plain word for non-Israelites. The Greek has the sentence of 32:19 in its 32:21 (see the variant), and the giants speak it there.

a: A sword has been handed over
t: A hard verse: who drags whom?
p: The Hebrew gives no clear subject. The Plain English Translation gives the words as they stand.
b: The Hebrew says: "among those killed by the sword they will fall; a sword is given; they have dragged her and all her multitudes." It is unclear who "they" are, who "her" is, and whether "they have dragged" should be read as a command ("drag her away"). The Greek is shorter: "in the midst of those pierced by the sword they will fall with him, and all his strength will sleep," with no dragging. In the Greek the words of Hebrew 32:19 come after this, in the speech of 32:21. The Plain English Translation gives a literal reading and leaves the shape of the sentence open. The sense for the whole is plain: Egypt, with her crowds, goes down to the dead.

p: Isaiah 14 has the same scene: the kings of the dead rise to meet a new arrival.
b: In Isaiah 14:9-11 the dead kings of Sheol rise from their thrones to greet the king of Babylon with the news that he has become as weak as they are. Ezekiel's scene is related: the mightiest of the fallen speak from Sheol, and the new arrival is laid among them. The ancient Near East had a similar picture of the dead below the earth, in Mesopotamian texts such as the Descent of Ishtar (Pritchard, Ancient Near Eastern Texts), where the dead live in dust. Ezekiel's scene is a prophetic satire, not a lesson on the afterlife. The fallen are ranked by how they died and were buried. Egypt, with its great cost of tomb and ritual for the king's afterlife, hears the opposite: shame among foreigners. In the Greek, "the giants" speak, and what they say includes the words of the Hebrew 32:19: "Whom are you better than? Go down and sleep with the uncircumcised."

p: Ezekiel names six groups. Some had already fallen, and some had not.
b: Assyria fell in 612 to 609 BC (see 31:11). Elam was crushed by Ashurbanipal about 646 BC; Jeremiah has a later word against Elam (Jeremiah 49:34-39). Meshech and Tubal were peoples of Anatolia, and are named again with Gog in 38:2-3. Edom (25:12-14) and Sidon (28:20-23) were alive in 585 BC; this is commonly explained as Ezekiel counting them dead because his oracles against them have been spoken. The six groups are Assyria, Elam, Meshech with Tubal, Edom, the leaders of the north and Sidon. "The leaders of the north" are not named further. The Greek replaces Edom (32:29) and the Sidonians (32:30) with the rulers and generals of Assyria.

p: The Hebrew says their guilt rests on their bones. A few modern readers think it said shields.
b: The Hebrew says "their iniquities (avonotam) were on their bones." The Greek has "their lawless acts were on their bones" and ends "they terrified all in their life." Whose "their" is, the Hebrew does not say: the nearest antecedent is the old warriors who went down with their weapons, and the closing "for the terror of those warriors" gives the reason; the verse can also be read as about Meshech and Tubal. Some modern commentators have proposed changing one word to read "their shields on their bones," which would fit the warriors buried with swords under their heads and shields over them. No manuscript read for this part has "shields," so the Plain English Translation keeps "guilt," the word all the witnesses have. The whole verse turns on its first word: the Hebrew has a negative ("they do not lie with the warriors"), the Greek has none ("they lay with the giants who fell of old"); see the variant. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, so the point is a contrast of burial: the old heroes lie in honor with their weapons, and Meshech and Tubal, who spread terror, do not. In 32:28 "you" is Pharaoh, named in 32:31-32.

p: Pharaoh is comforted at seeing others in the same ruin.
b: The word is nicham, to be comforted or to feel relief. It can mean relief at seeing justice done. In 14:22-23 the survivors of Jerusalem are "comforted" when they see how bad the wicked were. In 31:16 the trees of Eden are "comforted" when the cedar falls. The comfort in 32:31 is dark: Pharaoh sees the others in Sheol and is eased that he is not alone. The Plain English Translation keeps the word and leaves the irony to the reader.
